title: Dedicated SLOs: mapping customer expectations/commitments to proposed tiered SLOs (gaps + messaging)
content:
Owner: Lauren Bishop (PM Dedicated)
Last edit: 2026-02-14
Audience: Dedicated PM, SRE (Sean/Rafael/Aisha), Support/CS escalation (Rachel/Owen), Platform (Ethan/Mina)

Purpose
- Map what we currently imply/commit for Dedicated (sales/support language + common customer assumptions) to the proposed tiered SLOs + error budget policy.
- Identify gaps vs current observed performance (where we’re likely to miss on paper).
- Provide recommended customer-facing messaging that is accurate and sets expectations without reopening commercial SLAs (commercial changes are explicitly out of scope for this initiative).

Important framing
- This doc is NOT a contract rewrite. It’s an expectation alignment + comms plan that should reduce “surprise” escalations.
- Dedicated means: isolated capacity + predictable throughput and change control options. It does NOT guarantee “no incidents,” and it does not eliminate model-level variance.
- Proposed SLOs are service-level objectives used operationally and surfaced in Console; enterprise SLAs may be different and handled separately.

Sources used (informal)
- Recent Support escalations: SUP-3911 (p99 latency + intermittent 5xx), SUP-3950 (request for documented SLOs + behavior during incidents)
- Common sales narratives in Dedicated one-pagers (not attached here; summarized below)
- Early SRE strawman SLO tables + Dedicated readiness notes

1) What customers believe they are buying (current expectation inventory)
Below is a consolidation of what we repeatedly see in Dedicated deals, onboarding calls, and escalations. Some of these are written promises; most are implied.

A. Availability expectations
1) “Dedicated should basically never be down.”
2) “If you gave us isolated GPUs, why are we seeing 5xx?”
3) “We expect a defined uptime target and a clear incident comms process.”

B. Latency expectations
1) “Dedicated should be faster than Hosted.” (or at least more stable)
2) “We care about p99 and tail spikes, not averages.”
3) “Streaming latency should be measured as time-to-first-token (TTFT), not the full stream duration.”

C. Capacity/readiness expectations
1) “If we reserved capacity, it should always be ready.”
2) “Scaling should happen without us noticing.”
3) “We need an explicit definition of ‘pool ready’ / ‘warm’ and what happens on GPU/node failure.”

D. Operational/process expectations
1) “If you roll out a bad change, it shouldn’t impact our Dedicated pool.”
2) “There should be change control / canaries / coordinated maintenance.”
3) “During an incident, we want to know whether you will degrade quality (fallback models / throttling) and how you decide.”

2) Proposed Dedicated SLOs (what we plan to publish operationally)
NOTE: Final numbers live in Confluence tiered SLO definitions; this section focuses on how they map to expectations and where we’re most exposed.

2.1 SLO dimensions we should explicitly publish for Dedicated
- Inference API availability (success rate / 5xx / timeout) for:
  - Chat/completions streaming
  - Chat/completions non-streaming
  - Embeddings
- Latency SLOs per endpoint type:
  - Streaming: TTFT p95/p99 (and optionally “stream completion rate”)
  - Non-streaming: end-to-end p95/p99
  - Embeddings: p95/p99
- Streaming disconnect rate:
  - Server-side disconnects (counted)
  - Client aborts (excluded)
- Dedicated pool readiness SLO (new for this program):
  - “Pool Ready” signal (scheduler healthy + sufficient warm capacity) over a rolling window

2.2 Mapping table (expectations -> SLO/definition -> what we’ll say)

Expectation: “Dedicated should never be down”
- Proposed operational mapping:
  - Dedicated inference availability SLO (rolling 28d) measured at Redwood edge/gateway for the customer’s dedicated routes.
  - Exclusions: invalid auth, bad requests, customer-side timeouts/disconnects, customer network issues.
- Messaging:
  - “Dedicated is designed for high availability and predictable performance, with isolation from multi-tenant load. We publish an availability SLO per Dedicated pool and route. Some classes of failures (e.g., client aborts) are excluded so that the metric reflects Redwood-controlled reliability.”

Expectation: “Dedicated should be faster/more stable than Hosted”
- Proposed operational mapping:
  - Latency SLOs for TTFT and non-streaming e2e, broken down by region + model family.
  - We do not promise Dedicated will always have lower median latency than Hosted for every model; we do expect lower variance and fewer overload-induced spikes.
- Messaging:
  - “Dedicated optimizes for consistency: stable tail latency and predictable throughput. If your app’s primary pain is p99 spikes from shared capacity, Dedicated is the right tier. If your goal is the lowest possible median latency across many models, Hosted may be comparable depending on region/model.”

Expectation: “If we reserved capacity, it should always be ready”
- Proposed operational mapping:
  - Dedicated pool readiness SLO (separate from inference availability).
  - Define readiness precisely: control plane has assigned capacity, scheduler healthy, warm replicas above minimum, and routing can send traffic.
- Messaging:
  - “We report pool readiness separately from request success. This makes provisioning/maintenance visible and gives an earlier signal before request-level impact. Readiness dips can occur during GPU/node replacement; our goal is to keep inference availability within SLO even during these events.”

Expectation: “Don’t change things under us / coordinated rollouts”
- Proposed operational mapping:
  - Error budget policy enforcement + release gates for services that affect Dedicated (gateway, routing, control plane).
  - Canary + progressive rollout guardrails informed by budget burn.
- Messaging:
  - “We use an error-budget policy to prevent risky changes when reliability is trending poorly. When budgets are at risk, we automatically narrow rollouts and prioritize stability.”

Expectation: “During incidents, do you degrade quality?”
- Proposed operational mapping:
  - Routing mitigation policies: region failover and compatible fallback models are possible, but Dedicated guardrails apply.
  - For Dedicated, we should treat fallback as opt-in per customer/pool (or at least explicitly documented).
- Messaging:
  - “By default, Dedicated prioritizes correctness and isolation. Fallbacks that may change model behavior are configurable. During severe incidents, we may apply protective measures (e.g., queue limits) to preserve availability; any behavior that changes outputs should be agreed ahead of time.”

3) Where we have gaps vs current performance (risk register)
This section is intentionally blunt so we don’t publish targets that we can’t meet consistently.

3.1 Tail latency (p99) is our biggest Dedicated perception risk
- Evidence (qualitative): SUP-3911 and multiple CS notes show p99 spikes are what triggers escalations.
- Likely drivers:
  - Autoscaling lag / cold replicas after deployment or node replacement
  - Micro-bursts in customer traffic that exceed per-pool concurrency assumptions
  - Long-context requests creating queueing + KV cache pressure
  - Model-specific variance (some large instruction-tuned models show high TTFT tail)
- Proposed mitigation / how to frame:
  - Publish TTFT-based streaming SLOs (avoid the “full stream duration” argument).
  - Add guidance in Dedicated onboarding about concurrency + context-length distributions.
  - In Console, show p99 + saturation signals next to latency to explain “why.”

3.2 Pool readiness metric is new; we need to avoid creating a pager storm
- Concern:
  - If readiness is too sensitive, we’ll page on transient provisioning blips that never impact inference.
  - If it’s too lax, it won’t be useful as a leading indicator.
- Suggested approach:
  - Start with ticketing + dashboard visibility; page only on sustained readiness loss or when correlated with request SLO burn.
  - Make “readiness dips” part of the customer comms vocabulary only after we’re confident in the signal.

3.3 Error budget policy could be misinterpreted as “you stop working when things break”
- Customer risk:
  - “Change freeze” language can read as Redwood choosing process over customer urgency.
- Messaging guidance:
  - Emphasize that the policy still allows reliability fixes and explicitly defines an exception path.
  - Explain it as a guardrail against regressions, not a refusal to act.

3.4 Dedicated vs Hosted comparability and region/model carve-outs
- We should anticipate “why is my Dedicated SLO not the same as Hosted?”
- Suggested stance:
  - Dedicated SLOs are scoped to the customer’s pool and committed region/model set.
  - If a customer requests expanding to a new region/model, we may treat that as “new surface area” with separate SLO baselining.

4) Recommended customer-facing language (draft snippets)
These are intended for Support macros, CS QBR decks, and a short “Reliability for Dedicated” help-center style doc.

4.1 2–3 sentence summary
“Dedicated provides isolated GPU capacity and a dedicated routing path so you get predictable throughput and stable tail latency. We publish service-level objectives (SLOs) for availability and latency, and we use an error budget policy to prevent risky changes when reliability is trending poorly. During incidents, our mitigation actions prioritize keeping your service available, with configurable options for failover and fallbacks.”

4.2 What we measure (plain-English)
- Availability: “Did Redwood successfully accept and complete your request?”
- Latency: “How long did it take to start responding (TTFT for streaming) and to complete (for non-streaming/embeddings)?”
- Streaming disconnects: “Did the stream end unexpectedly due to a Redwood-side issue?”
- Pool readiness: “Is your dedicated pool in a healthy, ready state to serve traffic right now?”

4.3 What’s excluded (must be explicit)
“We exclude issues outside Redwood’s control (invalid requests/auth, customer-side timeouts, and client-aborted streams) so the SLO reflects platform reliability rather than client/network behavior.”

4.4 Comms during incidents (Dedicated-specific)
- If request-level SLO is at risk/exhausted: status update with “impact scope” (region + model + pool) + mitigations underway.
- If only readiness is degraded but inference SLO is holding: internal notification first; customer notification only if it is likely to affect throughput/latency.
- Avoid saying “error budget exhausted” as the headline; translate into customer impact:
  - “We are seeing elevated error rate/latency and are temporarily restricting changes while we stabilize.”

4.5 FAQ bullets Support can use
Q: “Does Dedicated guarantee lower latency than Hosted?”
A: “Dedicated is primarily about consistency and isolation. For some models/regions, median latency can be similar, but Dedicated significantly reduces multi-tenant contention and improves predictability. We publish p95/p99 targets for the pool.”

Q: “If you’re out of error budget, do you stop deploying fixes?”
A: “No. Reliability fixes are explicitly allowed. The policy restricts non-essential changes and expansions until stability is restored, and it has an exception path for urgent issues.”

Q: “Will you automatically switch my model during an incident?”
A: “Not without configuration. Dedicated prioritizes output stability and isolation. Fallbacks that may alter behavior are available as an opt-in policy.”

5) Action items / next steps
PM (Dedicated)
- Align with SRE on what we will publish as Dedicated readiness SLO vs internal-only signal for the first iteration.
- Work with Console PM (Marissa/Paula) to ensure Dedicated views show: pool selector, model list, region, availability/latency, and a clear “what’s excluded” info drawer.

SRE/Platform
- Confirm the exact SLI definitions for:
  - TTFT vs full stream latency
  - Streaming disconnect classification (client abort vs server fault)
  - Timeouts attribution (gateway vs upstream runtime)
- Validate readiness SLI robustness and proposed alerting thresholds (start ticket-only; page criteria TBD).

Support/CS
- Convert the messaging snippets into:
  - A Support macro for “Request for Dedicated SLOs” (SUP-3950-like)
  - A one-page customer explainer (no numbers if legal/commercial sensitivity; link to Console where the numbers live)

6) Open questions (need resolution before broad publication)
1) Do we publish Dedicated latency SLO targets at a single number, or per model family (recommended: per model family or at least per “large vs medium” categories)?
2) How do we handle multi-region Dedicated customers: one SLO per region or aggregate? (My take: per region, with an optional aggregate view.)
3) For customers with custom policy (no fallbacks, strict change windows), do we need a separate “Dedicated+” internal tier? (May be overkill; could be config-level.)
4) What’s the customer-facing explanation for readiness dips that don’t impact request success? We need consistent language that doesn’t look like we’re hiding instability.

Appendix A: Suggested structure for a Dedicated reliability page in docs/Console
- Overview: what Dedicated optimizes for
- SLOs shown in Console (availability, latency, disconnects, readiness)
- What’s excluded and why
- Incident communications: what to expect
- Optional policies: failover, fallback models, throttling behavior
- How to contact Support during an incident (Dedicated escalation path)

Appendix B: Notes from Support escalations (high level)
- SUP-3911: Customer flagged p99 spikes; primary ask was “define expectations and show us what you see.” They did not ask for credits; they asked for predictability.
- SUP-3950: Customer asked for documented SLOs and how error budgets affect behavior during incidents; they want to know if gating delays fixes or increases stability.
